household: with her uncle Will Fitzgerald and his ward Jericho Jones; Mabel Rose and her parents, Theta Knight and Henry DuBois live in the same building
creator: Libba Bray
address_as_given: the Bennington, a faded apartment building off Broadway
notes: The Bennington is a fictional building with 'gothic towers.' The novel puts it on the Upper West Side: Evie walks out of it onto Broadway, and Memphis sees its towers through the leaves as he walks toward Central Park West and 88th Street. No street or number is given, so the point is a neighborhood centroid. The source2 text is an unofficial upload of the novel on archive.org.
source_quote: Mabel, just like Will and Jericho, lives at the Bennington where Evie befriends Theta Knight, a Ziegfeld girl and her best friend Henry, a musician.
source2_quote: Evie left the Bennington and walked down Broadway, past the shops.

household: with his younger brother Isaiah, in their Aunt Octavia's apartment
creator: Libba Bray
address_as_given: Octavia's apartment in Harlem
notes: Memphis lives with Isaiah in their aunt Octavia's apartment in Harlem. The novel moves him around Lenox Avenue and 136th Street but gives the apartment no street, so the point is a Harlem centroid.
source_quote: Memphis – lives in Harlem, once had the ability to heal

creator: Kathleen Rooney
address_as_given: Murray Hill
notes: The elderly former Macy's ad writer sets out from her Murray Hill apartment on New Year's Eve 1984; the character is loosely based on the copywriter Margaret Fishback. No street is given in the sources found, so the point is a neighborhood centroid. She has lived in the neighborhood for decades by 1984; the setting years cover only the walk.
source_quote: Kathleen Rooney’s new novel, Lillian Boxfish Takes a Walk (St. Martin’s Press) follows the life of the red-headed poet of Murray Hill.

household: with her husband, the novelist James Gooch
creator: Candace Bushnell
address_as_given: One Fifth Avenue
notes: The novel is set inside the real 1927 Art Deco co-op at One Fifth Avenue, at Washington Square North. Mindy, head of the co-op board, resents that her family has the building's 'worst' apartment.
source_quote: Long resentful of the fact that her family inhabits One Fifth’s “worst” apartment, Mindy pushes through a quickie sale of Louise’s place seemingly just to thwart Enid.
source2_quote: She is the outsider looking in, even though she resides at One Fifth.

household: her nephew, the screenwriter Philip Oakland, also lives in the building
creator: Candace Bushnell
address_as_given: One Fifth Avenue
notes: The octogenarian gossip columnist is one of the building's longtime residents and a neighbor of the late Louise Houghton, whose penthouse sets off the plot. The quote names her among the Greenwich Village neighbors; the review is about the building at One Fifth Avenue.
source_quote: her Greenwich Village neighbors are anxious to have a say in who ends up living in her coveted 7,000 square-foot space. The players include octogenarian gossip columnist Enid Merle, her successful screenwriter nephew Philip Oakland

creator: Candace Bushnell
address_as_given: the penthouse at One Fifth, with a domed ballroom
notes: The Rices buy Louise Houghton's penthouse after her death.
source_quote: her historical penthouse at One Fifth with a domed ballroom and a 360-degree view of Manhattan, the race to see who can acquire the coveted real estate first begins.
source2_quote: The new residents, Paul and Annalisa Rice, certainly seem suitable.

creator: Caroline Kepnes
address_as_given: her Bank Street address, a West Village apartment
geocode_query: Bank Street and West 4th Street, Manhattan
notes: Joe finds Beck's Bank Street address online and watches her ground-floor apartment through its uncurtained windows. No house number is given; the point is the middle of Bank Street. Joe's own apartment is not placed in the sources found.
source_quote: From these, he learns her Bank Street address, her daily routines, her financial struggles, and her social circle. He begins watching her West Village apartment through uncurtained windows.

household: a rented room three flights up in Mrs. Osborne's house
creator: Patricia Highsmith
address_as_given: Sixty-third Street
geocode_query: East 63rd Street and Lexington Avenue, Manhattan
notes: Therese tells Carol she lives on Sixty-third Street; the novel gives no number. East Side is inferred: she rides home to the Lexington Avenue stop, like her coworker Mrs. Robichek on East 55th. The novel names no year; it is set around 1950. Carol's own house is in New Jersey and is out of scope.
source_quote: “Where do you live? In Manhattan?” Therese told her. On Sixty-third Street.
source2_quote: They found they both got off at the Lexington Avenue stop, too, though Mrs. Robichek lived on Fifty-fifth Street, just east of Third Avenue.

household: alone, with a tenant, David Winters, in the basement
creator: A. J. Finn
address_as_given: a four-level townhouse on her Harlem street
notes: The agoraphobic Dr. Anna Fox watches the street from the windows of her four-story Harlem townhouse. No street is named in the sources found.
source_quote: A new family is moving in on her Harlem street, and Dr. Anna Fox already knows their names, employment histories, how much they paid for their house
source2_quote: She has not left her four-level Harlem townhouse in nearly a year.

work: The Dark Tower II: The Drawing of the Three
creator: Stephen King
address_as_given: a renovated Victorian off Central Park South
geocode_query: Central Park South and 7th Avenue, Manhattan
notes: The wealthy heiress and civil rights activist; Roland draws her from 1964. The placement comes from a Reactor chapter-by-chapter reading of the novel, not from the text itself. Her other personality, Detta Walker, keeps a separate loft in Greenwich Village (see the next record).
source_quote: We learn that Andrew, the driver, is white, and Odetta is black and wealthy—she has a renovated Victorian off Central Park South.

household: the second personality of Odetta Holmes
work: The Dark Tower II: The Drawing of the Three
creator: Stephen King
address_as_given: the loft of an aging apartment building in Greenwich Village
notes: Detta keeps her own loft, unknown to Odetta, in an old Village building. No street is given, so the point is a neighborhood centroid. Eddie Dean, the novel's other New Yorker, was not placed by any source found.
source_quote: Detta Walker, unlike Odetta Holmes—has no interest in the civil rights movement. She lives in the loft of an aging apartment building in Greenwich Village.

household: with her mother, Mrs. Connage, and her brother Alec
creator: F. Scott Fitzgerald
address_as_given: the Connage house on Sixty-eighth Street, New York
notes: Rosalind's debut and her romance with Amory Blaine play out in the family house. The novel does not say East or West 68th Street; the point assumes the East Side, between Fifth and Park, as fits a rich family, and the radius is wide. Amory's own shared apartment with Tom and Alec is not placed.
source_quote: The place is a large, dainty bed room in the Connage house on Sixty-eighth Street, New York.

household: with the co-op's other residents: the super Vlade Marovich, Franklin Garr, Inspector Gen Octaviasdottir, Amelia Black, the quants Mutt and Jeff, and the boys Stefan and Roberto
creator: Kim Stanley Robinson
address_as_given: the old Met Life tower on Madison Square
notes: In a half-drowned Manhattan, the 1909 Met Life tower at 23rd Street and Madison is a co-op housing thousands, with a boathouse, farm floors and an airship mast. Most main characters live there, so this is one record for the household. A Locus commenter questioned whether the book meant a different MetLife building, but the novel names Madison Square.
source_quote: a brick-thick but buoyant survey of life among the residents of the Met Life tower at 23rd and Madison, now a canal-straddled co-op housing thousands, complete with boathouse, rooftop farm, and airship dock.
source2_quote: The old Met Life tower on the drowned remains of Madison Square is home, now, to several thousand souls

household: with her mother, a fortune teller
creator: Ami McKay
address_as_given: a squalid tenement on Chrystie Street
geocode_query: Chrystie Street and Delancey Street, Manhattan
notes: Twelve-year-old Moth lives with her mother in a Chrystie Street tenement until her mother sells her into service. No number is given; the point is the middle of Chrystie Street. Sara D. Roosevelt Park, opened in the 1930s, replaced the tenements on the street's east side.
source_quote: In 1871, in a squalid tenement on Chrystie Street, 12-year-old Moth Fenwick lives with her mother, a fortune teller whose affections Moth craves and never receives.

creator: Stephanie Clifford
address_as_given: the Upper East Side
notes: Evelyn's mother pays extra so that Evelyn's apartment has a socially acceptable Upper East Side address. No street was found, so the point is a neighborhood centroid.
source_quote: free herself from the influence of her social-climbing mother, who propelled her through prep school and onto the Upper East Side.

household: with her husband Russell Calloway and their twins
creator: Jay McInerney
address_as_given: a rented loft in Tribeca
notes: The Calloways' rented, one-bathroom Tribeca loft is their home in Bright, Precious Days (set 2006 to 2008) and is the 'downtown' loft of The Good Life (2006, set 2001 to 2002). No street was found. Where they lived in Brightness Falls (1992, set 1987) was not placed by any source found.
source_quote: Appallingly, the Calloways have been renters, the family of four still living in a loft in Tribeca without doorman, spa or gym
source2_quote: Corrine lives with her husband and two children in a downtown New York City loft.

creator: Thomas Wolfe
address_as_given: the Hotel Leopold, on a short and grimy street about two blocks from the university, northward, in the direction of Union Square
notes: The Leopold is invented. 'The university' is the novel's 'School for Utility Cultures,' standing in for New York University at Washington Square, where Wolfe taught from 1924. Two blocks north toward Union Square puts it around University Place and East 10th Street. The source text is a Digital Library of India scan on archive.org.
source_quote: THE Hotel Leopold, where he now lived, was situated on a short and grimy street about two blocks from the university, northward, in the direction of Union Square.

household: her grandmother's house, with her brother Prieto
creator: Xóchitl González
address_as_given: her grandma's house on Fifty-third Street
notes: Olga and Prieto grow up in their grandmother's house in Sunset Park, the neighborhood Prieto later represents in Congress. The novel gives 53rd Street without a cross street, so the point is the middle of 53rd Street's run through Sunset Park. The setting years are an estimate: Olga is about 40 in the 2017 present and leaves when she starts her wedding business.
source_quote: So, she moved out of her grandma’s house on Fifty-third Street and into a floor-through of a brownstone on a tree-lined street just a stone’s throw from Fort Greene Park

creator: Xóchitl González
address_as_given: a floor-through of a brownstone on a tree-lined street just a stone's throw from Fort Greene Park
notes: Olga's adult home as a high-end wedding planner. No street is named; the point sits beside Fort Greene Park. The start year is an estimate.
source_quote: into a floor-through of a brownstone on a tree-lined street just a stone’s throw from Fort Greene Park, one quick subway ride to Manhattan.

household: with his parents Tommy and Marie and his younger brother Albert
creator: Richard Price
address_as_given: the Bronx's Co-op City housing projects
notes: The De Coco family lives in Co-op City, the giant cooperative development in the northeast Bronx. No building or section is named in the sources found.
source_quote: The family in question is the de Cocos, residents of the Bronx’s Co-op City housing projects, and our protagonist is the clan’s eldest son, Stony
source2_quote: Wandering Co-op City, he gets into a fight with a night watchman and decides to stick with construction work.

household: with his son Andy and their housekeeper, Gerd
creator: David Gilbert
address_as_given: an apartment opposite the Frick Museum on Manhattan's Upper East Side
geocode_query: Fifth Avenue and East 71st Street, Manhattan
notes: The reclusive novelist lives in an apartment his mother bought him as a wedding present; the narrator, Philip Topping, later camps there too. 'Opposite the Frick' (Fifth Avenue between East 70th and 71st Streets) points to a building across East 70th or 71st Street. The novel is set in the present day; the year is an estimate.
source_quote: The grouchy A. N. Dyer lives with his third son, Andy, and their housekeeper, Gerd, in faded patrician grandeur opposite the Frick Museum on Manhattan’s Upper East Side
